explanation: Systematics is the study of the diversity of organisms using data ranging from the cellular to the population level. A primary goal of systematics is to determine the phylogeny, or evolutionary history, of a group. This history is typically depicted using a phylogenetic tree, which is a diagram showing lines of descent. Each branching point on the tree represents a divergence from a common ancestor and indicates an ancestral organism that gave rise to two or more new groups. Modern biological classification is designed to reflect this phylogeny by analyzing characters: ancestral traits are present in all members of a group and in their common ancestor, while derived traits are unique to only some members of a group and were absent in their common ancestor.

questions.q: What represents the divergence from a common ancestor on a phylogenetic tree?
opts: The terminal tips of the branches
The horizontal lines of the tree only
questions.exp: Each branching point (node) on a phylogenetic tree represents a divergence from a common ancestor, showing where one lineage split into two or more new groups.

questions.q: What is the difference between ancestral and derived traits?
opts: Ancestral traits are present in all group members and the common ancestor; derived traits are only in some members and absent in the common ancestor.
Ancestral traits are acquired during life; derived traits are coded in DNA.
Ancestral traits only occur in bacteria; derived traits only occur in eukaryotes.
Ancestral traits are homologous; derived traits are analogous.
questions.exp: Ancestral traits are shared by all members because they were inherited from the common ancestor, whereas derived traits evolved later and are present in only a subset of the group.
